topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the World Through Different Perspectives

outline.topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the World Through Different Perspectives

sections.title: The Concept of Perspective
sections.content: Introduce the idea that the same physical point in space can be described by different sets of coordinates depending on the observer's orientation. Use a character to ground the concept.
sections.example: Character 'Pixel the Robot' is standing in a room. From our perspective (Standard Basis), Pixel is at (3, 2). But from Pixel's own tilted perspective, he might feel like he is just 2 units forward and 1 unit left. The point is the same; the labels are different.

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: The Standard Basis
sections.content: Briefly review how we usually describe vectors as linear combinations of the standard unit vectors i (1,0) and j (0,1). Use a standard square grid visual.
sections.example: Visualizing the vector [3, 2] as 3 steps along the x-axis and 2 steps along the y-axis. These axes are our 'language' for space.

sections.title: Defining a New Basis
sections.content: Introduce a new set of basis vectors, B = {v1, v2}. Explain that for these to be a basis, they must be linearly independent (not pointing in the same line). Transform the square grid into a tilted/stretched grid.
sections.example: Let v1 = [2, 1] and v2 = [-1, 1]. In our world, these are arrows. In 'Pixel's World', these are his new unit steps. Animation shows the standard grid morphing into this new slanted coordinate system.

sections.title: The Translation Problem
sections.content: Explain the core goal: How do we translate 'Pixel's coordinates' into 'Our coordinates'? Introduce the notation [x]B for coordinates in the new basis and x for standard coordinates.
sections.example: If Pixel says he is at [2, 1] in his basis, we calculate: 2 * (his v1) + 1 * (his v2). Graphically, we follow his tilted arrows to find the final landing spot on our grid.

sections.title: The Change of Basis Matrix (P)
sections.content: Show that the translation process is just matrix multiplication. The 'Change of Basis Matrix' P is formed by placing the new basis vectors into the columns of a matrix.
sections.example: Matrix P = [[2, -1], [1, 1]]. If Pixel's coordinate is [2, 1], we multiply P * [2, 1]^T to get [3, 3]^T in our standard system. Animation highlights the columns of P being the basis vectors.

sections.title: The Reverse Journey (P-Inverse)
sections.content: Explain how to go from our world back to Pixel's world using the inverse matrix. This is crucial for understanding how different systems communicate.
sections.example: If we want to tell Pixel where a point (5, 4) is in his language, we use the inverse of P. Calculation: [x]B = P⁻¹ * x. Visual shows 'undoing' the tilt of the grid to return to a standard square view.

sections.title: Summary and Real-world Application
sections.content: Summarize that Change of Basis is just a 'dictionary' between two languages of space. Mention why we do this: some problems are easier to solve in a specific basis (like Eigenvectors or image compression).
sections.example: Mention JPEG compression: It changes the basis of image pixels into a 'frequency basis' where it's easier to throw away unimportant data without us noticing.

storyboard.title: The Concept of Perspective
lecture_lines: Meet Pixel the Robot standing in a room.
We see Pixel at coordinates (3, 2).
But from Pixel's view, his position feels different.
animations: Display a 2D coordinate system with a bright point at (3, 2) (#00FFFF).
Fade in 'Pixel the Robot' at the origin, tilted 30 degrees.
Draw a second, tilted coordinate system aligned with Pixel's body.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Check: The Standard Basis
lecture_lines: We usually describe space using standard unit vectors.
The vector i and j form our standard grid.
Every point is a combination of these base steps.
animations: Show a standard white square grid on the black background.
Animate the unit vectors i (1,0) in #FF5555 and j (0,1) in #55FF55.
Draw the vector [3, 2] by moving 3 units right then 2 units up.

storyboard.title: Defining a New Basis
lecture_lines: Imagine Pixel defines his own set of basis vectors.
These new vectors must be linearly independent.
They form a tilted and stretched coordinate grid.
Let's look at Pixel's world versus our own.
The same point now has two different labels.
animations: Plot vectors v1=[2, 1] in #FFFF00 and v2=[-1, 1] in #00FFFF.
Show the vectors are not collinear by extending them into dashed lines.
Label the set {v1, v2} as Basis "B".
Morph the square grid into a skewed grid defined by these vectors.
Highlight one slanted "unit cell" of the new grid.

storyboard.title: The Translation Problem
lecture_lines: How do we translate Pixel's coordinates to ours?
We follow his tilted arrows on our standard grid.
This calculation bridges the two different perspectives.
animations: Display a vector in the skewed grid and label it [2, 1]_B (#FFFFFF).
Show the sum: 2 * v1 + 1 * v2 visually with vector addition.
Fade in the standard grid to reveal the resulting point (3, 3).

storyboard.title: The Change of Basis Matrix (P)
lecture_lines: This translation is neatly handled by matrix multiplication.
We build matrix P using Pixel's basis vectors.
Each column of P is one of his vectors.
Multiplying P by Pixel's coordinates gives our coordinates.
P acts as a dictionary between these two languages.
animations: Show a 2x2 matrix P with placeholders.
Move vector v1 into the first column and v2 into the second.
Highlight the columns with colors matching the vectors (#FFFF00, #00FFFF).
Display the equation x = P * [x]_B at the top.
Animate a vector in B-coordinates transforming to standard coordinates via multiplication.

storyboard.title: The Reverse Journey (P-Inverse)
lecture_lines: What if we want to translate our coordinates back?
We need the inverse of our transition matrix, P.
Multiplying by P-inverse converts our view to Pixel's.
This operation 'undoes' the grid's tilt and stretch.
Now we can communicate back into Pixel's language.
animations: Start with the equation x = P * [x]_B.
Multiply both sides by P^-1 to get [x]_B = P^-1 * x.
Show the inverse matrix P^-1 appearing on screen.
Input a standard vector [5, 4] into the inverse transformation.
Show the grid "un-skewing" to find the coordinates in basis B.

storyboard.title: Summary and Real-world Application
lecture_lines: Change of basis is a tool for changing perspective.
It makes complex problems much easier to solve.
This concept powers technologies like JPEG image compression.
animations: Show a "Standard Basis" grid and a "Custom Basis" grid side-by-side.
Display icons for "Physics", "Computer Graphics", and "Data Compression".
Final text: "Change of Basis: A new way to see space."
